definition: The highest traded price during the preceding 52 weeks.
whyItMatters: It is a common reference for momentum, resistance, and investor anchoring.

definition: The lowest traded price during the preceding 52 weeks.
whyItMatters: It is a common reference for downside momentum, support, and drawdown.

definition: Amounts owed to suppliers for purchases already received.
whyItMatters: Payables provide operating financing but cannot grow indefinitely.

definition: Amounts customers owe for recognized sales not yet collected.
whyItMatters: Rapid receivable growth can weaken cash conversion or signal credit risk.

definition: A period in which informed or persistent buying absorbs available supply.
whyItMatters: Accumulation is inferred from behavior and cannot be known from price alone.

definition: Purchase of control of a company or business.
whyItMatters: The buyer's value depends on price paid, integration, and realized economics.

definition: A portfolio's return minus its benchmark return.
whyItMatters: It isolates the result of deviating from the benchmark.

definition: A cumulative measure of advancing issues minus declining issues.
whyItMatters: Divergence from an index may reveal strengthening or weakening breadth.

definition: Trading after the primary exchange's regular session.
whyItMatters: Earnings reactions often occur here, with heightened gap and liquidity risk.

definition: An instruction not to execute unless the full requested quantity can be filled.
whyItMatters: It may delay or prevent fills in less liquid securities.

definition: The highest recorded market price for a security.
whyItMatters: Breaks to new highs remove historical overhead supply but do not guarantee continuation.

definition: Return beyond that implied by a selected risk model or benchmark.
whyItMatters: It separates skill or unexplained performance from systematic exposure.

sections.title: Formula
sections.body: Simple alpha = Portfolio return − Expected return from the chosen model

sections.title: Variables
sections.body: Portfolio return is the observed result; expected return is the result implied by the chosen benchmark or factor model.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.body: A 12% return against a model expectation of 9% implies 3% alpha.

sections.title: Interpretation and limitation
sections.body: Alpha is model-dependent and can reflect omitted risks, luck, or bad benchmarking.

definition: A U.S.-traded certificate representing shares of a foreign company.
whyItMatters: ADRs add currency, custody, political, and home-market risks.

definition: Allocation of an intangible asset or financing cost over time.
whyItMatters: Different types have different implications for recurring economics.

definition: Overreliance on an initial number or reference point.
whyItMatters: Purchase price and old highs can distort a fresh assessment of value.

definition: Return standard deviation scaled to a one-year horizon.
whyItMatters: It enables rough comparison across assets and sampling frequencies.

sections.title: Formula
sections.body: Annualized volatility ≈ Periodic standard deviation × √Periods per year

sections.title: Variables
sections.body: Periodic standard deviation uses returns at one frequency; periods per year is commonly 252 for daily or 12 for monthly observations.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.body: A 1% daily standard deviation gives about 15.9% annualized volatility using 252 days.

sections.title: Interpretation and limitation
sections.body: Square-root scaling assumes stable, weakly dependent returns and can fail in crises.

definition: Higher highs and higher lows oscillate between two roughly parallel rising boundaries.
whyItMatters: This bullish trend channel formation provides a structured way to define confirmation and invalidation.

sections.title: Confirmation
sections.body: Trend continuation is supported while pullbacks hold the lower channel; an upper break can accelerate.

sections.title: Invalidation
sections.body: A sustained close below the lower channel breaks the rising structure.

sections.title: Measured target
sections.body: Use the opposite channel boundary first; on breakout, project the channel height upward.

sections.title: Practical caution
sections.body: Treat the diagram as a schematic. Confirm the real price structure, timeframe, liquidity, and volume rather than matching a shape mechanically.

definition: Repeated tests of flat resistance occur while each reaction low rises.
whyItMatters: This bullish compression / breakout formation provides a structured way to define confirmation and invalidation.

sections.title: Confirmation
sections.body: Price closes above horizontal resistance after the range contracts.

sections.title: Invalidation
sections.body: Price breaks the rising support line and fails to recover it.

sections.title: Measured target

sections.title: Practical caution
sections.body: Treat the diagram as a schematic. Confirm the real price structure, timeframe, liquidity, and volume rather than matching a shape mechanically.

definition: The lowest displayed price at which a seller is willing to sell.
whyItMatters: A buyer crossing the spread normally executes near the ask.

definition: The division of capital among asset classes or exposure groups.
whyItMatters: Allocation usually drives more portfolio risk than individual security selection.

definition: A group of investments with similar economic characteristics and risk drivers.
whyItMatters: Asset allocation decisions are commonly made at the asset-class level.

definition: The obligation imposed on an option writer when a holder exercises.
whyItMatters: American-style options can be assigned before expiration.

definition: An option whose strike is near the underlying price.
whyItMatters: Time value and gamma are often most important near at-the-money strikes.

definition: Judging likelihood by how easily examples come to mind.
whyItMatters: Vivid news can overwhelm base rates and broader evidence.

definition: A volatility indicator based on the largest of three daily range measures.
whyItMatters: ATR helps scale stops and position sizes to current volatility.

definition: Contracted or ordered work not yet recognized as revenue.
whyItMatters: Backlog may improve visibility but can be canceled, delayed, or low margin.

definition: A snapshot of assets, liabilities, and shareholders' equity at a date.
whyItMatters: It reveals financing, liquidity, and accumulated capital.

definition: The historical frequency of an outcome in a relevant reference class.
whyItMatters: Base rates provide a starting point before company-specific adjustments.

definition: A sharp flagpole decline is followed by a short, orderly upward-sloping channel.
whyItMatters: This bearish continuation formation provides a structured way to define confirmation and invalidation.

sections.title: Invalidation

sections.title: Practical caution

definition: A sustained market decline, commonly described as a fall of at least 20% from a recent peak.
whyItMatters: Drawdowns often change correlations, liquidity, and investor behavior.

definition: A sharp decline is followed by a small contracting consolidation with converging boundaries.
whyItMatters: This bearish continuation formation provides a structured way to define confirmation and invalidation.

sections.title: Invalidation

sections.title: Measured target
sections.body: Project the flagpole length downward from the pennant breakout.

sections.title: Practical caution
sections.body: Treat the diagram as a schematic. Confirm the real price structure, timeframe, liquidity, and volume rather than matching a shape mechanically.

whyItMatters: It can mark a shift in control after an advance or at resistance.

whyItMatters: This bearish continuation formation provides a structured way to define confirmation and invalidation.

sections.title: Invalidation
sections.body: Price rises above range resistance or cannot stay below a failed breakdown.

sections.title: Measured target
sections.body: Project the rectangle height downward from the support break.

sections.title: Practical caution
sections.body: Treat the diagram as a schematic. Confirm the real price structure, timeframe, liquidity, and volume rather than matching a shape mechanically.

definition: Study of how cognitive and emotional biases affect financial decisions and markets.
whyItMatters: Recognizing predictable errors can improve process even when they cannot be eliminated.

definition: Qualitative summary of economic conditions across Federal Reserve districts, published before policy meetings.
whyItMatters: Scheduled releases matter mainly through the surprise versus expectations and the change in the expected economic path.

sections.title: Publisher and cadence
sections.body: Federal Reserve

sections.title: How to read it
sections.body: Look for changes in activity, labor availability, wages, prices, credit, and regional breadth.

sections.title: Typical market channels
sections.body: Policy narratives, banks, regional activity, and confirmation of survey trends.

sections.title: Caution
sections.body: It is anecdotal and descriptive, not a statistically representative forecast.

definition: A reference index or return series used to evaluate a portfolio.
whyItMatters: The benchmark should reflect the portfolio's investable opportunity set and risk.

definition: A broker's duty to seek the most favorable reasonably available execution terms.
whyItMatters: Price improvement, speed, likelihood, and total cost all matter.

definition: The estimated sensitivity of a security's returns to benchmark returns.
whyItMatters: It summarizes historical market exposure for portfolio and cost-of-equity work.

sections.title: Formula
sections.body: Beta = Covariance(asset, market) ÷ Variance(market)

sections.title: Variables
sections.body: Covariance measures joint asset and benchmark returns; variance measures benchmark-return dispersion over the same observations.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.body: A beta of 1.3 implies an estimated 1.3% move for each 1% benchmark move, on average.

sections.title: Interpretation and limitation
sections.body: Beta depends on benchmark, window, frequency, leverage, and changing regimes.

definition: The highest displayed price at which a buyer is willing to buy.
whyItMatters: A seller crossing the spread normally executes near the bid.

definition: The difference between the best bid and best ask.
whyItMatters: A wider spread increases the implicit cost of entering and exiting.

definition: A moving average surrounded by bands set a chosen number of standard deviations away.
whyItMatters: Band width and price location describe volatility and relative extension.

definition: A debt security representing a contractual promise to pay interest and repay principal.
whyItMatters: Bond yields influence discount rates, financing costs, and equity valuations.

definition: Bookings divided by recognized revenue or billings for the same period.
whyItMatters: A ratio above one can indicate expanding demand and backlog.

definition: The value of customer orders or contracts signed during a period.
whyItMatters: Bookings can be a leading indicator of future revenue.

definition: A downside move through a defined support or pattern boundary.
whyItMatters: Failed breakdowns can reverse sharply when sellers are trapped.

definition: A move beyond a defined resistance, support, range, or pattern boundary.
whyItMatters: Confirmation, volume, and follow-through help distinguish a breakout from noise.

definition: Higher highs and lower lows expand volatility between diverging boundaries.
whyItMatters: This neutral compression / breakout formation provides a structured way to define confirmation and invalidation.

definition: A regulated investment company that finances smaller or developing businesses.
whyItMatters: BDCs can provide high income but carry credit and leverage risk.

definition: Owning investments through market fluctuations for a long horizon.
whyItMatters: It minimizes trading friction but still requires thesis and risk review.

definition: A contract giving the holder the right, not the obligation, to buy the underlying at the strike price.
whyItMatters: Calls provide leveraged upside with a finite life and premium at risk.

definition: Cash spent to acquire or improve long-lived assets.
whyItMatters: Maintenance and growth capex affect free cash flow differently.

definition: A burst of intense selling that reflects investors giving up on positions.
whyItMatters: It can occur near a low but is recognizable only imperfectly in real time.

definition: A statement reconciling cash changes across operating, investing, and financing activities.
whyItMatters: It helps test whether accounting earnings convert into cash.

definition: A short put backed by enough cash to purchase shares if assigned.
whyItMatters: It earns premium while accepting the obligation to buy at the strike.

definition: An identifiable event that could cause the market to reassess a security.
whyItMatters: A catalyst can shorten the time between thesis and price realization.

definition: The rate at which customers or recurring revenue are lost.
whyItMatters: Small churn changes can materially affect subscription economics.

definition: A rule that pauses trading after specified market moves or abnormal conditions.
whyItMatters: Pauses allow information and orders to rebalance during disorderly markets.

definition: A pooled fund with a generally fixed share count that trades on an exchange.
whyItMatters: Its market price can remain above or below its net asset value.

definition: An exchange process that matches orders to establish the official closing price.
whyItMatters: Index funds and institutional benchmarks create heavy closing-auction volume.

definition: Short-term unsecured debt issued by corporations.
whyItMatters: Stress in commercial paper can signal tightening short-term funding conditions.

definition: A standardized raw material such as oil, copper, wheat, or gold.
whyItMatters: Commodity prices can affect company margins, inflation, and sector performance.

definition: Equity ownership that usually carries voting rights and a residual claim on assets and earnings.
whyItMatters: Common shareholders receive value after creditors and preferred shareholders.

definition: A valuation method using trading multiples of similar public companies.
whyItMatters: Peer selection and metric consistency strongly influence the result.

definition: The constant annual rate that links a beginning value to an ending value over multiple years.
whyItMatters: It summarizes multi-period growth in one comparable number.

sections.title: Formula
sections.body: CAGR = (Ending value ÷ Beginning value)^(1 ÷ Years) − 1

sections.title: Variables
sections.body: Beginning and ending values use the same metric and units; years is the number of compounding intervals between them.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.body: Growth from 100 to 161.05 in five years equals a 10% CAGR.

sections.title: Interpretation and limitation
sections.body: CAGR hides volatility and the path between endpoints.

definition: Net income plus specified gains and losses recorded outside net income.
whyItMatters: It captures some economic changes omitted from the income statement.

definition: A large share of a portfolio invested in a small number of exposures.
whyItMatters: Concentration increases both upside participation and loss severity.

definition: Preference for evidence that supports an existing belief.
whyItMatters: Actively seeking disconfirming evidence improves thesis quality.

definition: The aggregated forecast of surveyed economists or analysts.
whyItMatters: Markets usually react to the difference between reported data and expectations.

definition: Monthly survey of household views on current conditions and expectations.
whyItMatters: Scheduled releases matter mainly through the surprise versus expectations and the change in the expected economic path.

sections.title: How to read it
sections.body: Separate present conditions from expectations and compare labor perceptions with spending data.

sections.title: Typical market channels
sections.body: Consumer sectors, recession views, housing, and discretionary demand.

sections.title: Caution
sections.body: Attitudes can respond to politics and gasoline prices without equal spending changes.

definition: Taking positions against prevailing sentiment after independent analysis.
whyItMatters: Being different is useful only when the consensus is actually wrong.

definition: A bond that may be converted into a specified number of issuer shares.
whyItMatters: It combines credit exposure with equity upside and dilution potential.

definition: A meaningful decline, commonly 10% or more, that is smaller than the conventional bear-market threshold.
whyItMatters: Corrections are normal but can expose leverage and weak risk controls.

definition: The degree to which two return series move together.
whyItMatters: Diversification benefits depend on correlations, which can rise during crises.

definition: Direct costs attributable to producing goods or delivering services sold.
whyItMatters: Its relationship to revenue determines gross profit.

definition: A scale-dependent measure of how two variables vary together.
whyItMatters: It is an input to portfolio variance and optimization.

definition: Long shares combined with a short call on those shares.
whyItMatters: It earns premium in exchange for capping upside and retaining most downside.

definition: Monthly consumer-price inflation for a basket of goods and services.
whyItMatters: Scheduled releases matter mainly through the surprise versus expectations and the change in the expected economic path.

sections.title: Publisher and cadence
sections.body: Bureau of Labor Statistics

sections.title: How to read it
sections.body: Compare headline and core monthly rates, breadth, shelter, services, revisions, and consensus.

sections.title: Typical market channels
sections.body: Treasury yields, policy expectations, the dollar, rate-sensitive growth stocks, housing, and consumer margins.

sections.title: Caution
sections.body: One month can be noisy; base effects and seasonal adjustment can distort annual comparisons.

definition: The yield difference between a risky debt instrument and a comparable benchmark.
whyItMatters: Widening spreads can signal rising default risk and tighter financial conditions.

definition: A position held by many investors with similar reasons and exit triggers.
whyItMatters: Even a sound thesis can suffer when positioning unwinds abruptly.

definition: A rounded cup returns to prior resistance, followed by a smaller controlled handle pullback.
whyItMatters: This bullish reversal formation provides a structured way to define confirmation and invalidation.

sections.title: Confirmation
sections.body: Price closes above the cup rim after holding the handle structure.

sections.title: Invalidation
sections.body: Price breaks the handle low or falls back deeply into the cup.

sections.title: Measured target
sections.body: Project the cup depth upward from the rim breakout.

sections.title: Practical caution
sections.body: Treat the diagram as a schematic. Confirm the real price structure, timeframe, liquidity, and volume rather than matching a shape mechanically.

definition: Current assets relative to current liabilities.
whyItMatters: It is a basic measure of near-term balance-sheet coverage.

sections.title: Formula
sections.body: Current ratio = Current assets ÷ Current liabilities

sections.title: Variables
sections.body: Current assets are expected to convert to cash within the operating cycle or one year; current liabilities are obligations due over the same horizon.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.body: $2B current assets divided by $1B current liabilities equals 2.0×.

sections.title: Interpretation and limitation
sections.body: Inventory quality, credit lines, seasonality, and cash conversion matter beyond the ratio.

definition: Sales and marketing cost required to acquire a new customer.
whyItMatters: It should be evaluated against customer lifetime value and payback time.

definition: Estimated contribution generated by a customer over the relationship.
whyItMatters: Optimistic retention or margin assumptions can make the metric misleading.

definition: Sensitivity of business results to economic or industry cycles.
whyItMatters: Peak-cycle earnings can make a cyclical company appear deceptively cheap.

definition: An order that expires if it is not filled by the end of the trading session.
whyItMatters: It prevents an old instruction from carrying into another session.

definition: Short interest divided by average daily trading volume.
whyItMatters: A high value suggests shorts may need more time to exit.

definition: A bearish moving-average crossover, commonly the 50-day average moving below the 200-day average.
whyItMatters: It is lagging and may occur after much of a decline.

definition: Debt relative to shareholders' equity.
whyItMatters: It gives a simple view of balance-sheet leverage.

sections.title: Formula
sections.body: Debt-to-equity = Total debt ÷ Shareholders' equity

sections.title: Variables
sections.body: Total debt is interest-bearing borrowing; shareholders' equity is the accounting residual attributable to owners.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.body: $3B debt divided by $2B equity equals 1.5×.

sections.title: Interpretation and limitation
sections.body: Negative or unusually small book equity makes the ratio unreliable.

definition: Cash received before the related revenue is recognized.
whyItMatters: It can provide financing and visibility but is accompanied by a delivery obligation.

definition: A sustained decline in the general price level.
whyItMatters: It can increase real debt burdens and discourage spending or investment.

definition: The approximate change in option price for a one-unit change in the underlying, all else equal.
whyItMatters: It also describes directional exposure and changes with price and time.

definition: Allocation of a tangible asset's cost over its useful life.
whyItMatters: It lowers accounting profit and signals the consumption of productive assets.

definition: Lower highs and lower lows oscillate between two roughly parallel falling boundaries.

sections.title: Invalidation
sections.body: A sustained close above the upper channel breaks the falling structure.

sections.title: Measured target
sections.body: Use the opposite channel boundary first; on breakdown, project the channel height downward.

sections.title: Practical caution
sections.body: Treat the diagram as a schematic. Confirm the real price structure, timeframe, liquidity, and volume rather than matching a shape mechanically.

definition: The required return used to convert future cash flows into present value.
whyItMatters: Small rate changes can materially affect long-duration valuations.

definition: A valuation method that discounts forecast cash flows to present value.
whyItMatters: It makes growth, margins, reinvestment, and required return assumptions explicit.

definition: A slowing rate of inflation while the price level continues to rise.
whyItMatters: Markets may respond differently to disinflation than to outright deflation.

definition: The tendency to sell winners too early and hold losers too long.
whyItMatters: It can weaken risk-adjusted returns and tax efficiency.

definition: A period in which persistent selling transfers shares to other buyers.
whyItMatters: Distribution can precede weakness but requires confirmation.

definition: A disagreement between price direction and an indicator or related series.
whyItMatters: Divergence is a warning condition, not a standalone timing signal.

definition: Spreading exposure across investments with different risk drivers.
whyItMatters: It can reduce idiosyncratic risk but cannot eliminate market risk.

definition: A distribution of corporate value to shareholders, usually paid in cash or shares.
whyItMatters: Yield alone does not show whether the payment is sustainable.

definition: The share of earnings distributed as dividends.
whyItMatters: It helps assess dividend coverage and retained reinvestment capacity.

sections.title: Formula
sections.body: Payout ratio = Common dividends ÷ Common net income

sections.title: Variables
sections.body: Common dividends are distributions declared for common owners; common net income is profit attributable to those owners for the same period.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.body: $300M dividends on $500M common earnings equals 60%.

sections.title: Interpretation and limitation
sections.body: For some sectors, free-cash-flow payout or distributable cash flow is more informative.

definition: A program that uses dividends to purchase additional shares.
whyItMatters: It automates compounding but does not remove valuation or concentration risk.

definition: Expected annual dividend per share relative to share price.
whyItMatters: It measures indicated cash income before taxes and reinvestment.

sections.title: Formula
sections.body: Dividend yield = Annual dividend per share ÷ Share price

sections.title: Variables
sections.body: Annual dividend per share is the indicated recurring distribution over one year; share price is the current price.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.body: $2 annual dividends on a $50 share equal a 4% yield.

sections.title: Interpretation and limitation
sections.body: A high yield may signal a pending cut; use sustainable forward dividends.

definition: A candlestick with nearly equal opening and closing prices.
whyItMatters: It signals indecision and needs location and follow-through for meaning.

definition: Investing a fixed amount at regular intervals regardless of price.
whyItMatters: It reduces timing dependence but does not guarantee a profit.

definition: Two comparable lows are separated by a clear reaction high after a decline.
whyItMatters: This bullish reversal formation provides a structured way to define confirmation and invalidation.

sections.title: Confirmation
sections.body: Price closes above the reaction-high neckline after the second bottom.

sections.title: Invalidation
sections.body: Price closes back below the two-trough support zone.

sections.title: Measured target
sections.body: Project the neckline-to-support height upward from the break.

sections.title: Practical caution
sections.body: Treat the diagram as a schematic. Confirm the real price structure, timeframe, liquidity, and volume rather than matching a shape mechanically.

definition: Two comparable highs are separated by a clear reaction low after an advance.
whyItMatters: This bearish reversal formation provides a structured way to define confirmation and invalidation.

sections.title: Confirmation
sections.body: Price closes below the reaction-low neckline after the second top.

sections.title: Invalidation
sections.body: Price closes back above the two-peak resistance zone.
