sections.body: Project the resistance-to-neckline height downward from the break.

sections.title: Practical caution
sections.body: Treat the diagram as a schematic. Confirm the real price structure, timeframe, liquidity, and volume rather than matching a shape mechanically.

definition: The possibility and severity of returns below a target or acceptable threshold.
whyItMatters: Investors often experience losses asymmetrically compared with gains.

definition: A price structure generally characterized by lower highs and lower lows.
whyItMatters: Rallies inside a downtrend may remain countertrend until structure changes.

definition: The decline from a portfolio or security's prior peak to a subsequent trough.
whyItMatters: Drawdown measures the lived path of losses rather than average variability.

definition: Monthly new orders for long-lasting manufactured goods.
whyItMatters: Scheduled releases matter mainly through the surprise versus expectations and the change in the expected economic path.

sections.title: Publisher and cadence
sections.body: U.S. Census Bureau

sections.title: How to read it
sections.body: Separate volatile aircraft and defense orders and inspect core capital-goods orders and shipments.

sections.title: Typical market channels
sections.body: Industrials, transports, business-investment expectations, and GDP tracking.

sections.title: Caution
sections.body: Large aircraft orders make the headline exceptionally volatile.

definition: The risk that an American-style short option is exercised before expiration.
whyItMatters: It rises around dividends and when remaining time value is small.

definition: Operating-oriented profit before financing cost and income tax.
whyItMatters: EBIT helps compare operations across capital structures.

definition: A management presentation and question-and-answer session accompanying results.
whyItMatters: Commentary can reveal drivers, risks, and changes not obvious in headline numbers.

definition: Net income attributable to common shareholders expressed per weighted-average diluted share.
whyItMatters: EPS connects company profit with each share and is central to P/E valuation.

sections.title: Formula
sections.body: Diluted EPS = Common net income ÷ Diluted weighted-average shares

sections.title: Variables
sections.body: Common net income is profit attributable to common owners; diluted weighted-average shares reflects the time-weighted share count plus dilutive instruments.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.body: $500M of common net income across 250M diluted shares equals $2.00 EPS.

sections.title: Interpretation and limitation
sections.body: Buybacks, dilution, one-time items, and accounting choices can change EPS without equal operating change.

definition: A company's periodic report of financial results and business updates.
whyItMatters: Price reactions depend on results versus expectations and the revised outlook.

definition: The difference between reported earnings and the consensus estimate.
whyItMatters: A beat or miss matters in relation to quality, guidance, and priced expectations.

definition: Earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization.
whyItMatters: It is a common operating proxy but is not cash flow.

definition: A durable advantage that protects returns from competition.
whyItMatters: A real moat can sustain margins, growth, and reinvestment opportunities.

definition: A market in which available information is rapidly incorporated into prices.
whyItMatters: The idea frames the difficulty of earning persistent risk-adjusted excess returns.

definition: Valuing an asset more highly merely because it is owned.
whyItMatters: Owners may demand more evidence to sell than they required to buy.

definition: The value attributed to a company's operating assets for all capital providers.
whyItMatters: It supports comparisons using pre-financing operating metrics.

sections.title: Formula
sections.body: EV = Equity value + Debt + Preferred stock + Noncontrolling interest − Cash

sections.title: Variables
sections.body: Equity value is common market capitalization; debt includes interest-bearing obligations; cash is excess cash and equivalents; preferred stock and noncontrolling interest are non-common claims.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.body: A $12B market cap plus $3B debt and $1B cash produces about $14B EV.

sections.title: Interpretation and limitation
sections.body: Adjustments vary; restricted cash, leases, pensions, and investments require judgment.

definition: Enterprise value divided by EBITDA.
whyItMatters: It compares operating value before capital structure, tax, and noncash charges.

sections.title: Formula
sections.body: EV/EBITDA = Enterprise value ÷ EBITDA

sections.title: Variables
sections.body: Enterprise value represents all operating capital claims; EBITDA is earnings before interest, tax, depreciation, and amortization for the matching period.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.body: $15B EV divided by $1.5B EBITDA equals 10×.

sections.title: Interpretation and limitation
sections.body: EBITDA is not cash flow and the multiple can hide capital expenditure and working-capital needs.

definition: A three-candle bearish reversal sequence with strength, hesitation, then a strong decline.
whyItMatters: The third candle provides evidence that sellers regained control.

definition: The first date a buyer is not entitled to the declared dividend under normal settlement.
whyItMatters: The stock price commonly adjusts for the distribution, all else equal.

definition: A pooled fund whose shares trade on an exchange throughout the day.
whyItMatters: ETFs provide diversified or targeted exposure with stock-like execution.

definition: Use of an option right to buy or sell the underlying at the strike.
whyItMatters: Exercise can create stock, cash, tax, and funding consequences.

definition: Monthly count of completed sales of previously owned homes.
whyItMatters: Scheduled releases matter mainly through the surprise versus expectations and the change in the expected economic path.

sections.title: Publisher and cadence
sections.body: National Association of Realtors

sections.title: How to read it
sections.body: Inventory, months of supply, prices, and mortgage-rate sensitivity matter with the headline.

sections.title: Typical market channels
sections.body: Housing-linked equities, brokers, lenders, renovation, and consumer durables.

sections.title: Caution
sections.body: Closings lag purchase agreements and the series is not an official government release.

definition: The final date on which an option retains contractual life.
whyItMatters: Time value normally decays as expiration approaches.

definition: A moving average that gives greater weight to recent observations.
whyItMatters: It reacts faster than a same-length simple moving average.

sections.title: Formula
sections.body: EMA today = Price today×k + EMA prior×(1−k), where k = 2/(n+1)

sections.title: Variables
sections.body: n is the selected lookback; k is the smoothing factor; EMA prior is the preceding period's exponential average.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.body: A 10-period EMA uses a smoothing factor of 2/11, or about 18.18%.

sections.title: Interpretation and limitation
sections.body: Faster response also increases sensitivity to noise.

definition: Price makes lower highs and lower lows inside two falling, converging boundaries.
whyItMatters: This bullish compression / breakout formation provides a structured way to define confirmation and invalidation.

sections.title: Confirmation
sections.body: Price closes above the upper wedge boundary with upside follow-through.

sections.title: Invalidation
sections.body: Price loses the upper boundary and breaks below the wedge low.

sections.title: Measured target
sections.body: Project the wedge’s widest height upward from the breakout.

sections.title: Practical caution
sections.body: Treat the diagram as a schematic. Confirm the real price structure, timeframe, liquidity, and volume rather than matching a shape mechanically.

definition: A move beyond a level that quickly returns inside the prior structure.
whyItMatters: Waiting for confirmation can reduce, but not eliminate, false-signal risk.

definition: Anxiety-driven buying motivated by others' gains or rapidly rising prices.
whyItMatters: It encourages poor entries, oversized positions, and abandoned risk controls.

definition: The overnight U.S. interbank rate targeted by the Federal Reserve.
whyItMatters: It anchors short-term funding costs and influences broader financial conditions.

definition: Horizontal reference levels based on selected Fibonacci ratios applied to a price move.
whyItMatters: Traders watch them as potential reaction zones, not causal laws.

definition: The execution of all or part of an order.
whyItMatters: Average fill price and filled quantity determine the realized trade.

definition: An order requiring the entire quantity to fill immediately or be canceled.
whyItMatters: It avoids partial positions but sharply reduces execution probability.

definition: Use of debt or fixed financing claims in a company's capital structure.
whyItMatters: It can raise equity returns but also default and refinancing risk.

definition: Government taxation and spending decisions.
whyItMatters: Fiscal changes can affect growth, inflation, sector demand, and public borrowing.

definition: Shares available for public trading after excluding closely held or restricted shares.
whyItMatters: A small float can amplify volatility and price impact.

definition: Target-rate decision and policy statement, normally eight scheduled times per year.
whyItMatters: Scheduled releases matter mainly through the surprise versus expectations and the change in the expected economic path.

sections.title: Publisher and cadence
sections.body: Federal Reserve

sections.title: How to read it
sections.body: Compare the decision, statement, projections, and press conference with what rates markets expected.

sections.title: Typical market channels
sections.body: Front-end Treasury yields, the dollar, valuation multiples, banks, housing, and broad risk appetite.

sections.title: Caution
sections.body: A nominally unchanged rate can still be hawkish or dovish; market positioning often dominates the first reaction.

definition: Detailed account of a prior policy meeting, normally released with a lag.
whyItMatters: Scheduled releases matter mainly through the surprise versus expectations and the change in the expected economic path.

sections.title: Publisher and cadence
sections.body: Federal Reserve

sections.title: How to read it
sections.body: Look for the range of views, risk balance, and conditions members attached to future action.

sections.title: Typical market channels
sections.body: Rates and currencies first, with equity effects through discount rates and growth expectations.

sections.title: Caution
sections.body: The minutes describe an older meeting and may be overtaken by newer data or speeches.

definition: A U.S. public company's comprehensive annual filing with audited statements and risk disclosures.
whyItMatters: It is a primary source for long-form fundamental analysis.

definition: A U.S. public company's quarterly filing with unaudited interim financial information.
whyItMatters: It updates financials, risks, and management discussion between annual reports.

definition: A U.S. filing used to report specified material events.
whyItMatters: It can disclose acquisitions, leadership changes, financings, and results promptly.

definition: Share price relative to forecast earnings per share.
whyItMatters: It embeds the market's view against near-term earnings expectations.

sections.title: Formula
sections.body: Forward P/E = Share price ÷ Forecast EPS

sections.title: Variables
sections.body: Share price is today's quote; forecast EPS is the expected per-share profit for a clearly identified future period.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.body: A $60 stock with expected EPS of $4 trades at 15× forward earnings.

sections.title: Interpretation and limitation
sections.body: Forecast error and differing estimate periods can make comparisons misleading.

definition: Cash generated after operating needs and capital expenditures.
whyItMatters: It is cash potentially available for debt reduction, distributions, acquisitions, or reinvestment.

sections.title: Formula
sections.body: FCF = Cash flow from operations − Capital expenditures

sections.title: Variables
sections.body: Cash flow from operations is operating cash generated; capital expenditures are cash purchases of property, equipment, and other long-lived operating assets.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.body: $800M operating cash flow less $300M capex equals $500M FCF.

sections.title: Interpretation and limitation
sections.body: Classifying capex, stock compensation, acquisitions, and working-capital swings requires judgment.

definition: Free cash flow relative to equity value or enterprise value, depending on the cash-flow definition.
whyItMatters: It translates cash generation into a valuation yield.

sections.title: Formula
sections.body: Equity FCF yield = Free cash flow to equity ÷ Market capitalization

sections.title: Variables
sections.body: Free cash flow to equity is cash available to common owners; market capitalization is the value of common equity.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.body: $500M FCF on a $10B market cap equals 5%.

sections.title: Interpretation and limitation
sections.body: Keep numerator and denominator consistent and normalize temporary cash-flow swings.

definition: Assessment of a security using business economics, financial statements, industry conditions, and valuation.
whyItMatters: It links an investment decision to the underlying enterprise rather than price alone.

definition: A standardized agreement to buy or sell an asset at a future date and price.
whyItMatters: Futures are leveraged and widely used for hedging and price discovery.

definition: The rate at which delta changes as the underlying price changes.
whyItMatters: High gamma creates rapidly changing directional exposure.

definition: A price interval between sessions in which no trading occurred.
whyItMatters: Gaps can mark new information, low liquidity, or important support and resistance.

definition: An opening below the prior session's trading range or close.
whyItMatters: Whether the gap fills or extends helps evaluate selling pressure.

definition: An opening above the prior session's trading range or close.
whyItMatters: Whether the gap holds helps evaluate demand after new information.

definition: Quarterly estimate of real economic output, released in advance, second, and third estimates.
whyItMatters: Scheduled releases matter mainly through the surprise versus expectations and the change in the expected economic path.

sections.title: Publisher and cadence
sections.body: Bureau of Economic Analysis

sections.title: How to read it
sections.body: Compare growth composition, price indexes, inventories, trade, and domestic final demand with expectations.

sections.title: Typical market channels
sections.body: Cyclicals, yields, policy expectations, earnings forecasts, and recession probabilities.

sections.title: Caution
sections.body: Headline GDP can be boosted by volatile inventories or trade while domestic demand weakens.

definition: A bullish moving-average crossover, commonly the 50-day average moving above the 200-day average.
whyItMatters: It is lagging and works best with broader trend confirmation.

definition: An order that remains open until filled, canceled, or expired by the broker.
whyItMatters: Long-lived orders should be reviewed as conditions change.

definition: An acquisition asset representing purchase price above identifiable net assets.
whyItMatters: Impairment can reveal that expected acquisition benefits did not materialize.

definition: A terminal-value method assuming cash flow grows perpetually at a constant rate.
whyItMatters: It converts the post-forecast cash-flow stream into one value.

sections.title: Formula
sections.body: Terminal value = Next-period cash flow ÷ (Discount rate − Perpetual growth)

sections.title: Variables
sections.body: Next-period cash flow is the first cash flow after the forecast; discount rate is the required return; perpetual growth is the sustainable long-run growth rate.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.body: $105 cash flow with 8% discount and 3% growth gives $2,100 terminal value.

sections.title: Interpretation and limitation
sections.body: Growth must remain below the discount rate and be sustainable for the economy and business.

definition: Gross profit expressed as a percentage of revenue.
whyItMatters: It reflects product economics, pricing, input costs, and mix.

sections.title: Formula
sections.body: Gross margin = (Revenue − Cost of goods sold) ÷ Revenue

sections.title: Variables
sections.body: Revenue is recognized sales; cost of goods sold is the direct cost assigned to those sales.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.body: $400M gross profit on $1B revenue equals 40%.

sections.title: Interpretation and limitation
sections.body: Classification policies and business mix can limit comparisons.

definition: Revenue minus cost of goods sold.
whyItMatters: It shows the economic surplus available before operating expenses.

definition: Seeking companies expected to expand earnings or cash flow faster than peers.
whyItMatters: Growth stocks are often especially sensitive to expectations and discount rates.

definition: A candle with a small real body near the high and a long lower shadow after weakness.
whyItMatters: It can show rejection of lower prices when confirmed by subsequent action.

definition: A hammer-shaped candle appearing after an advance.
whyItMatters: Its context makes it a potential warning rather than a bullish reversal candle.

definition: Three peaks form after an advance; the middle head is highest and the shoulders are similar.
whyItMatters: This bearish reversal formation provides a structured way to define confirmation and invalidation.

sections.title: Confirmation
sections.body: A decisive close below the neckline, ideally with expanding volume.

sections.title: Invalidation
sections.body: Price reclaims the neckline and then closes above the right shoulder.

sections.title: Measured target
sections.body: Project the head-to-neckline height downward from the neckline break.

sections.title: Practical caution
sections.body: Treat the diagram as a schematic. Confirm the real price structure, timeframe, liquidity, and volume rather than matching a shape mechanically.

definition: Taking an offsetting exposure intended to reduce a specified risk.
whyItMatters: Hedges have costs, basis risk, and may reduce upside as well as downside.

definition: Following the actions of a group instead of relying on independent analysis.
whyItMatters: Crowds can aggregate information but also create crowded trades.

definition: Seeing an outcome as more predictable after it occurred.
whyItMatters: Decision journals help separate process quality from outcome knowledge.

definition: Volatility calculated from past underlying returns.
whyItMatters: Comparing it with implied volatility helps frame option richness, with important caveats.

definition: A preference for domestic investments beyond their weight in the global opportunity set.
whyItMatters: It can reduce currency complexity but increase geographic concentration.

definition: Monthly estimate of new residential construction starts and permits.
whyItMatters: Scheduled releases matter mainly through the surprise versus expectations and the change in the expected economic path.

sections.title: Publisher and cadence
sections.body: U.S. Census Bureau and HUD

sections.title: How to read it
sections.body: Permits lead starts; inspect single-family versus multifamily activity and regional volatility.

sections.title: Typical market channels
sections.body: Homebuilders, building products, mortgage sensitivity, banks, and cyclical growth.

sections.title: Caution
sections.body: Weather and small regional samples create large monthly swings.

definition: Company- or security-specific risk that can be reduced through diversification.
whyItMatters: A single position can damage a concentrated portfolio even when the market is stable.

definition: An order requiring any available quantity to fill immediately, with the remainder canceled.
whyItMatters: It is useful when delayed or resting exposure is undesirable.

definition: The volatility input consistent with an option's market price under a pricing model.
whyItMatters: It represents the price of expected uncertainty, not a guaranteed forecast.

definition: An option with positive intrinsic value.
whyItMatters: Moneyness affects delta, exercise value, and sensitivity to time decay.

definition: Prioritizing cash distributions such as dividends or interest.
whyItMatters: A high yield is only valuable when the payment and principal are sustainable.

definition: A statement of revenue, expenses, and profit over a period.
whyItMatters: It explains reported profitability but not necessarily cash generation.

definition: A fund designed to track a specified market index rather than select securities actively.
whyItMatters: Fees, tracking difference, and index methodology drive investor outcomes.

definition: Monthly output of manufacturing, mining, and utilities.
whyItMatters: Scheduled releases matter mainly through the surprise versus expectations and the change in the expected economic path.

sections.title: Publisher and cadence
sections.body: Federal Reserve

sections.title: How to read it
sections.body: Compare manufacturing breadth, capacity utilization, revisions, and weather-sensitive utilities.

sections.title: Typical market channels
sections.body: Industrials, commodities, margins, and cyclical growth expectations.

sections.title: Caution
sections.body: Utilities and mining can obscure the manufacturing signal.

definition: A sustained rise in the general price level.
whyItMatters: Inflation affects purchasing power, margins, interest rates, and valuation multiples.

definition: Active return divided by tracking error.
whyItMatters: It measures how consistently active risk produced excess return.

definition: Weekly count of new unemployment-insurance claims.
whyItMatters: Scheduled releases matter mainly through the surprise versus expectations and the change in the expected economic path.

sections.title: Publisher and cadence
sections.body: U.S. Department of Labor

sections.title: How to read it
sections.body: Use the trend and continuing claims rather than overreacting to one holiday-distorted week.

sections.title: Typical market channels
sections.body: Near-term labor and recession expectations, rates, and cyclical equities.

sections.title: Caution
sections.body: Eligibility rules, seasonality, disasters, and reporting backlogs can distort the series.

definition: The first public sale and listing of a company's shares.
whyItMatters: Limited history, lockups, allocation, and price discovery can create volatility.

definition: A candle whose high-low range sits within the preceding candle's range.
whyItMatters: It represents compression that can resolve in either direction.

definition: A purchase or sale by a company insider subject to disclosure rules.
whyItMatters: Transactions require context because diversification and compensation can drive them.

definition: Operating earnings available relative to interest expense.
whyItMatters: It indicates the cushion for servicing debt.

sections.title: Formula
sections.body: Interest coverage = EBIT ÷ Net interest expense

sections.title: Variables
sections.body: EBIT is earnings before interest and tax; net interest expense is interest cost after interest income when that convention is used.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.body: $600M EBIT divided by $100M interest equals 6× coverage.

sections.title: Interpretation and limitation
sections.body: Cyclical earnings, floating rates, maturities, and cash balances affect true credit capacity.

definition: An estimate of an asset's economic worth based on expected future benefits and risk.
whyItMatters: It provides a decision anchor independent of the current quote.

definition: Goods held for sale or used in production.
whyItMatters: Excess or obsolete inventory can cause markdowns and cash strain.

definition: An inverted rounded cup returns to support, followed by a smaller upward handle retracement.
whyItMatters: This bearish reversal formation provides a structured way to define confirmation and invalidation.

sections.title: Confirmation
sections.body: Price closes below the cup base after failing within the handle.

sections.title: Invalidation
sections.body: Price breaks the handle high or recovers deeply into the inverted cup.

sections.title: Measured target
sections.body: Project the inverted-cup height downward from the base breakout.

sections.title: Practical caution
sections.body: Treat the diagram as a schematic. Confirm the real price structure, timeframe, liquidity, and volume rather than matching a shape mechanically.

definition: Three troughs form after a decline; the middle head is lowest and the shoulders are similar.
whyItMatters: This bullish reversal formation provides a structured way to define confirmation and invalidation.

sections.title: Confirmation
sections.body: A decisive close above the neckline, ideally with expanding volume.

sections.title: Invalidation
sections.body: Price loses the neckline and then closes below the right shoulder.

sections.title: Measured target
sections.body: Project the neckline-to-head height upward from the neckline break.

sections.title: Practical caution
sections.body: Treat the diagram as a schematic. Confirm the real price structure, timeframe, liquidity, and volume rather than matching a shape mechanically.

definition: A candle with a small body near the low and a long upper shadow after a decline.
whyItMatters: Bullish confirmation is needed because sellers still pushed price off the high.

definition: The expected length of time an investment will be held.
whyItMatters: Horizon affects suitable volatility, liquidity, and valuation assumptions.

definition: A testable explanation for why an investment should deliver an attractive outcome.
whyItMatters: Clear drivers, valuation, catalysts, and invalidation conditions improve decisions.

definition: A limited-risk position combining an out-of-the-money call spread and put spread.
whyItMatters: It generally benefits when price remains within a range and implied volatility falls.

definition: Monthly survey diffusion index for U.S. manufacturing activity.
whyItMatters: Scheduled releases matter mainly through the surprise versus expectations and the change in the expected economic path.

sections.title: Publisher and cadence
sections.body: Institute for Supply Management

sections.title: How to read it
sections.body: Read new orders, production, employment, prices, and supplier deliveries around the 50 level.

sections.title: Typical market channels
sections.body: Industrials, materials, rates, earnings expectations, and broader risk appetite.

sections.title: Caution
sections.body: A diffusion index measures direction and breadth, not the percentage change in output.

definition: Monthly survey diffusion index for U.S. services activity.
whyItMatters: Scheduled releases matter mainly through the surprise versus expectations and the change in the expected economic path.

sections.title: Publisher and cadence
sections.body: Institute for Supply Management

sections.title: How to read it
sections.body: Compare business activity, new orders, employment, and prices with consensus and prior trends.

sections.title: Typical market channels
sections.body: Rates, domestic cyclicals, labor demand, and inflation-sensitive sectors.

sections.title: Caution
sections.body: Survey composition and the 50 threshold do not map directly to GDP growth.

definition: Monthly employment situation covering payrolls, unemployment, wages, hours, and participation.
whyItMatters: Scheduled releases matter mainly through the surprise versus expectations and the change in the expected economic path.

sections.title: Publisher and cadence
sections.body: Bureau of Labor Statistics

sections.title: How to read it
sections.body: Read payrolls with revisions, household employment, participation, wage growth, and workweek versus expectations.

sections.title: Typical market channels
sections.body: Growth expectations, policy pricing, rates, consumer sectors, staffing, and cyclicals.

sections.title: Caution
sections.body: Payroll and household surveys can diverge; weather, strikes, and seasonal factors create noise.

definition: Monthly estimates of job openings, hires, quits, and separations.
whyItMatters: Scheduled releases matter mainly through the surprise versus expectations and the change in the expected economic path.

sections.title: Publisher and cadence
sections.body: Bureau of Labor Statistics

sections.title: How to read it
sections.body: Openings and quits help assess labor demand and worker confidence relative to labor supply.

sections.title: Typical market channels
sections.body: Wage-pressure expectations, policy pricing, staffing firms, and cyclical sentiment.

sections.title: Caution
sections.body: The data are lagged, revised, and based on a survey with meaningful sampling uncertainty.

definition: Use of borrowing or derivatives to increase exposure relative to capital.
whyItMatters: Leverage magnifies returns and can force liquidation at the worst time.

definition: An instruction to trade only at a specified price or better.
whyItMatters: It controls price but may never execute or may fill only partially.

definition: The ability to trade promptly near the quoted price without materially moving the market.
whyItMatters: Poor liquidity raises spread, slippage, and exit risk.

definition: The risk that a position cannot be traded quickly near a reasonable price.
whyItMatters: Quoted prices may be unavailable when many investors seek the same exit.

definition: A period restricting specified insiders from selling shares after an offering or transaction.
whyItMatters: Expiration can increase available supply but does not ensure selling.

definition: The tendency to experience losses more strongly than equivalent gains.
whyItMatters: It can cause premature profit-taking and reluctance to exit failed positions.

definition: Deploying available capital at one time rather than in stages.
whyItMatters: It gains immediate market exposure but carries greater entry-timing risk.

definition: A company's forecast or qualitative outlook for future performance.
whyItMatters: Changes versus prior guidance and expectations often drive stock reactions.

definition: A brokerage account that permits borrowing against securities.
whyItMatters: Borrowing magnifies gains, losses, interest expense, and liquidation risk.

definition: A demand to add capital or reduce exposure after account equity falls below a requirement.
whyItMatters: Failure to meet it can lead to forced liquidation.

definition: The discount between price and a conservative estimate of value.
whyItMatters: It provides room for analytical error and adverse outcomes.

definition: The degree to which individual securities participate in a market move.
whyItMatters: Narrow leadership can make an index advance less robust than it appears.

definition: The market value of a company's outstanding equity.
whyItMatters: It is widely used to compare company size and construct indexes.

definition: Equity market value based on the current share price.
whyItMatters: It converts a per-share quote into total public equity value.

sections.title: Formula
sections.body: Market capitalization = Share price × Diluted shares outstanding

sections.title: Variables
sections.body: Share price is the current price per common share; diluted shares outstanding includes the expected effect of dilutive awards and securities.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.body: At $40 per share and 250 million shares, market capitalization is $10 billion.

sections.title: Interpretation and limitation
sections.body: Use a consistent diluted share count; market cap is not enterprise value.

definition: A recurring progression through expansion, peak, contraction, and recovery in prices or economic activity.
whyItMatters: Recognizing the cycle helps frame growth, valuation, and policy sensitivity.

definition: An instruction to trade immediately at the best available prices.
whyItMatters: It prioritizes execution certainty over price certainty.

definition: The prevailing attitude and risk appetite of market participants.
whyItMatters: Sentiment can drive valuation and positioning away from near-term fundamentals.

definition: A company's sales or units as a percentage of its defined market.
whyItMatters: Share trends help distinguish company execution from industry growth.

definition: A large-bodied candle with very small or absent shadows.
whyItMatters: It reflects strong directional control during that period.

definition: A publicly traded partnership, often used for energy infrastructure assets.
whyItMatters: Its distributions and tax reporting differ from ordinary corporate dividends.

definition: The largest peak-to-trough percentage decline in a return series.
whyItMatters: It conveys historical loss severity and recovery burden.

sections.title: Formula
sections.body: Maximum drawdown = Minimum[(Value ÷ Prior peak) − 1]

sections.title: Variables
sections.body: Value is the portfolio or price index at each observation; prior peak is the highest value observed before that point.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.body: A fall from 120 to 84 is a 30% drawdown.

sections.title: Interpretation and limitation
sections.body: It describes one historical path and does not bound future losses.

definition: Treating money differently based on arbitrary labels or sources.
whyItMatters: It can hide the portfolio's true combined risk and opportunity cost.

definition: A transaction combining two companies into one economic organization.
whyItMatters: Consideration, approvals, synergies, financing, and antitrust risk affect outcomes.

definition: The strength and persistence of price movement.
whyItMatters: Momentum can confirm a trend or diverge before a possible reversal.

definition: Favoring securities with strong recent relative or absolute performance.
whyItMatters: Momentum can persist but is vulnerable to abrupt factor reversals.

definition: Central-bank actions affecting money, credit, rates, and financial conditions.
whyItMatters: Policy changes alter discount rates, demand, currencies, and risk appetite.

definition: A volume-weighted momentum oscillator derived from price and volume.
whyItMatters: It adds participation information to an RSI-like framework.

definition: A fund holding high-quality short-term debt instruments.
whyItMatters: It is used for cash management but is not identical to an insured bank deposit.

definition: A three-candle bullish reversal sequence with weakness, hesitation, then a strong recovery.
whyItMatters: The third candle provides evidence that buyers regained control.

definition: A momentum indicator based on the difference between fast and slow exponential moving averages.
whyItMatters: Crossovers and histogram changes help describe trend momentum.

sections.title: Formula
sections.body: MACD = Fast EMA − Slow EMA; Histogram = MACD − Signal EMA

sections.title: Variables
sections.body: Fast and slow EMA are commonly 12 and 26 periods; the signal EMA is commonly a 9-period EMA of the MACD line.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.body: With a fast EMA of 105 and slow EMA of 100, MACD is +5 before the signal comparison.

sections.title: Interpretation and limitation
sections.body: It is lagging and can whipsaw in sideways markets.

definition: A decrease in the valuation multiple assigned to a financial metric.
whyItMatters: A company can grow earnings while its share price falls if the multiple contracts enough.

definition: An increase in the valuation multiple investors assign to a financial metric.
whyItMatters: Returns can exceed business growth when sentiment or rates lift the multiple.

definition: A pooled investment vehicle priced at net asset value, normally once per trading day.
whyItMatters: Its dealing mechanics differ from intraday-traded ETFs.

definition: Constructing a persuasive story that overstates causal understanding.
whyItMatters: A coherent narrative should still be tested against data and alternatives.

definition: Profit remaining after all recognized expenses, interest, and taxes.
whyItMatters: It belongs to shareholders but may differ materially from cash flow.

definition: Net income expressed as a percentage of revenue.
whyItMatters: It captures the final accounting profitability available to owners.

sections.title: Formula
sections.body: Net margin = Net income ÷ Revenue

sections.title: Variables
sections.body: Net income is bottom-line accounting profit; revenue is sales for the same period.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.body: $80M net income on $1B revenue equals 8%.

sections.title: Interpretation and limitation
sections.body: Taxes, financing, gains, and one-time items can obscure operating trends.

definition: Recurring revenue retained from an existing customer cohort after expansion, contraction, and churn.
whyItMatters: Values above 100% indicate expansion exceeds losses within the cohort.

definition: Monthly annualized estimate of new single-family home sales.
whyItMatters: Scheduled releases matter mainly through the surprise versus expectations and the change in the expected economic path.

sections.title: Publisher and cadence
sections.body: U.S. Census Bureau and HUD

sections.title: How to read it
sections.body: Compare supply, price mix, revisions, and regional breadth with mortgage-rate conditions.

sections.title: Typical market channels
sections.body: Homebuilders, building materials, mortgage finance, and housing-led growth.

sections.title: Caution
sections.body: The estimate has a wide confidence interval and is frequently revised.

definition: The portion of a consolidated subsidiary not owned by the reporting parent.
whyItMatters: Enterprise and equity value calculations must treat it consistently.

definition: A model-based estimate of current economic conditions before complete official data are available.
whyItMatters: It updates faster than traditional forecasts but remains uncertain and revision-prone.

definition: A cumulative indicator that adds volume on up closes and subtracts it on down closes.
whyItMatters: Its trend can help assess whether volume confirms price.

definition: The number of option contracts still open at the end of a reporting period.
whyItMatters: It indicates outstanding positioning but not whether traders are bullish or bearish.

definition: An exchange process that matches accumulated orders to establish an opening price.
whyItMatters: The auction can concentrate liquidity and overnight price discovery.

definition: Costs of running the business that are not included in cost of goods sold.
whyItMatters: Expense discipline affects operating leverage and profitability.

definition: Profit after operating costs but before interest and taxes.
whyItMatters: It focuses on the economics of core operations.

definition: The sensitivity of operating profit to revenue changes because some costs are fixed.
whyItMatters: It amplifies both earnings growth and earnings declines.

definition: Operating income expressed as a percentage of revenue.
whyItMatters: It shows profit from operations before financing and tax.

sections.title: Formula
sections.body: Operating margin = Operating income ÷ Revenue

sections.title: Variables
sections.body: Operating income is profit before financing and income tax; revenue is sales for the same period.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.body: $150M operating income on $1B revenue equals 15%.

sections.title: Interpretation and limitation
sections.body: Adjust consistently for restructuring, stock compensation, and unusual items.

definition: The immediate exercise value of an option, never below zero.
whyItMatters: It separates exercise value from time value in the premium.

definition: The price paid by an option buyer and received by its seller.
whyItMatters: Premium reflects intrinsic value, time, volatility, rates, and dividends.

definition: The number of option contracts traded during a period.
whyItMatters: Unusual volume can signal attention but requires context and trade-direction evidence.

definition: Growth generated by existing operations rather than acquisitions or currency translation.
whyItMatters: It is often a cleaner measure of underlying demand and execution.

definition: An option with no intrinsic value at the current underlying price.
whyItMatters: It must move favorably before expiration to finish with exercise value.

definition: A candle whose range exceeds both the high and low of the preceding candle.
whyItMatters: It signals range expansion but direction depends on close and context.

definition: Excessive belief in one's information, forecasts, or skill.
whyItMatters: It often leads to concentration, leverage, and unnecessary trading.

definition: Urgent selling driven primarily by fear during a decline.
whyItMatters: It can lock in losses without evaluating liquidity needs or thesis changes.

definition: Execution of only part of an order's requested quantity.
whyItMatters: Partial fills can leave unintended exposure or additional commissions.

definition: Compensation a broker receives for routing customer orders to a trading venue or market maker.
whyItMatters: It raises questions about execution quality and conflicts of interest.

definition: Monthly personal-consumption inflation using weights that adjust with consumer behavior.
whyItMatters: Scheduled releases matter mainly through the surprise versus expectations and the change in the expected economic path.

sections.title: Publisher and cadence
sections.body: Bureau of Economic Analysis

sections.title: How to read it
sections.body: Core PCE and its monthly pace are central to Federal Reserve analysis; compare with consensus and revisions.

sections.title: Typical market channels
sections.body: Policy expectations, bond yields, currencies, and equity valuation through real-rate expectations.

sections.title: Caution
sections.body: The release contains revisions and may largely reflect already published CPI and PPI components.

definition: A P/E ratio scaled by an earnings-growth rate.
whyItMatters: It provides a rough bridge between valuation and growth.

sections.title: Formula
sections.body: PEG = P/E ÷ EPS growth rate expressed as a whole percentage

sections.title: Variables
sections.body: P/E is the selected earnings multiple; EPS growth is entered as a whole percentage, so 12% is entered as 12 rather than 0.12.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.body: A 24× P/E with 12% growth gives a PEG of 2.0.

sections.title: Interpretation and limitation
sections.body: Growth definitions, cyclicality, and the arbitrary scaling make PEG only a screening aid.

definition: Uncertainty about exercise and assignment when the underlying closes near a strike at expiration.
whyItMatters: It can leave an unexpected stock position after the market closes.

definition: The amount of capital or risk assigned to an investment.
whyItMatters: Sizing converts an investment view into actual portfolio impact.

definition: Monthly prices received by domestic producers across stages of production.
whyItMatters: Scheduled releases matter mainly through the surprise versus expectations and the change in the expected economic path.

sections.title: Publisher and cadence
sections.body: Bureau of Labor Statistics

sections.title: How to read it
sections.body: Compare final-demand and underlying components with expectations and possible pass-through to consumers.

sections.title: Typical market channels
sections.body: Inflation expectations, margins, rates, industrial companies, and pricing-power narratives.

sections.title: Caution
sections.body: PPI composition differs from CPI and does not mechanically predict consumer inflation.

definition: Trading before the primary exchange's regular session.
whyItMatters: Liquidity is often thinner and spreads wider than during regular hours.

definition: A valuation method using prices paid in comparable acquisitions.
whyItMatters: Control premiums and cycle conditions can make deal multiples unlike public trading values.

definition: A hybrid security with priority over common stock for dividends and liquidation, often without voting rights.
whyItMatters: Its return profile can resemble both equity and fixed income.

definition: The current value of a future cash flow discounted for time and risk.
whyItMatters: It is the core building block of discounted valuation.

sections.title: Formula
sections.body: PV = Future cash flow ÷ (1 + Discount rate)^Periods

sections.title: Variables
sections.body: Future cash flow is the amount received later; discount rate is the required return per period; periods is the number of matching compounding intervals.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.body: $110 received in one year discounted at 10% has a $100 present value.

sections.title: Interpretation and limitation
sections.body: The correct discount rate must match the cash flow's risk and currency.

definition: The process through which buyers and sellers establish a market price.
whyItMatters: Transparent, liquid trading generally improves the quality of observed prices.

definition: The price movement caused by submitting or executing an order.
whyItMatters: Large orders may need to be staged to reduce market impact.

definition: Equity value relative to common shareholders' book value.
whyItMatters: It is often used for financial firms and asset-heavy businesses.

sections.title: Formula
sections.body: P/B = Market capitalization ÷ Common book value

sections.title: Variables
sections.body: Market capitalization is common equity value; common book value is assets minus liabilities and senior equity claims.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.body: A $12B market cap divided by $8B book value equals 1.5× book.

sections.title: Interpretation and limitation
sections.body: Accounting book value may poorly represent intangible-heavy or impaired assets.

definition: Share price relative to earnings per share.
whyItMatters: It shows how much investors pay for each unit of current or expected earnings.

sections.title: Formula
sections.body: P/E = Share price ÷ EPS

sections.title: Variables
sections.body: Share price and EPS must refer to the same share class; EPS may be trailing, forward, GAAP, or adjusted and must be labeled consistently.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.body: A $60 stock earning $3 per share trades at 20× earnings.

sections.title: Interpretation and limitation
sections.body: P/E is not meaningful with negative earnings and must be paired with growth, quality, and cycle context.

definition: Equity value relative to revenue.
whyItMatters: It is usable when earnings are small or negative, but ignores cost structure.

sections.title: Formula
sections.body: P/S = Market capitalization ÷ Revenue

sections.title: Variables
sections.body: Market capitalization is common equity value; revenue is company sales over a consistent trailing or forecast period.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.body: A $5B company with $1B revenue trades at 5× sales.

sections.title: Interpretation and limitation
sections.body: Margins, dilution, capital intensity, and revenue quality determine whether the multiple is sensible.

definition: The ability to raise prices without losing unacceptable demand.
whyItMatters: Pricing power can defend margins against inflation and competition.

definition: The market in which newly issued securities are sold by an issuer.
whyItMatters: Capital raised in a primary transaction goes to the issuer or selling holders.

definition: Long shares combined with a long put.
whyItMatters: It creates a downside floor for the cost of the put premium.

definition: A filing providing voting matters, governance, ownership, and executive compensation information.
whyItMatters: It helps evaluate incentives, dilution, and board accountability.

definition: A diffusion index derived from business surveys, with 50 commonly separating expansion from contraction.
whyItMatters: PMIs are timely indicators of economic direction and corporate conditions.

definition: A contract giving the holder the right, not the obligation, to sell the underlying at the strike price.
whyItMatters: Puts can express downside views or hedge existing shares.

definition: Favoring durable businesses with strong economics, balance sheets, and governance.
whyItMatters: Quality can reduce fundamental fragility but may command a high valuation.

definition: Central-bank asset purchases intended to add liquidity and lower longer-term yields.
whyItMatters: It can support financial conditions but its effects depend on context and expectations.

definition: Reduction of a central bank's securities holdings or balance-sheet support.
whyItMatters: It can withdraw liquidity and place upward pressure on term premiums.

definition: Liquid current assets relative to current liabilities.
whyItMatters: It excludes inventory to provide a stricter short-term liquidity view.

sections.title: Formula
sections.body: Quick ratio = (Cash + Marketable securities + Receivables) ÷ Current liabilities

sections.title: Variables
sections.body: Quick assets are cash, marketable securities, and collectible receivables; current liabilities are near-term obligations.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.body: $900M quick assets divided by $600M liabilities equals 1.5×.

sections.title: Interpretation and limitation
sections.body: Receivable quality and access to funding still matter.

definition: A sustained or sharp rise in a security or market.
whyItMatters: A rally can occur inside either a bull market or a longer bear market.

definition: A company or trust that owns or finances income-producing real estate under a qualifying tax structure.
whyItMatters: REITs offer listed real-estate exposure and often distribute substantial income.

definition: An interest rate adjusted for expected or realized inflation.
whyItMatters: Real rates influence consumption, investment, currencies, and equity duration.

definition: Restoring a portfolio toward target weights by trading or directing new cash.
whyItMatters: Rebalancing controls drift and can impose a buy-low, sell-high discipline.

definition: Overweighting recent events when judging future probabilities.
whyItMatters: Recent performance may be mistaken for a durable regime.

definition: A broad and meaningful contraction in economic activity.
whyItMatters: Recessions usually pressure earnings and credit while prompting policy responses.

definition: The date on which the company identifies shareholders entitled to a distribution or vote.
whyItMatters: Settlement timing links eligibility to the ex-dividend date.

definition: The time required to regain a prior peak after a drawdown.
whyItMatters: Deep losses require disproportionately large gains and can impair compounding.

definition: Revenue expected to repeat under subscriptions, contracts, or repeat-purchase behavior.
whyItMatters: Durability and renewal economics matter more than the label alone.

definition: A feedback loop in which market perceptions influence fundamentals, which then influence perceptions.
whyItMatters: Prices can affect financing, confidence, and business outcomes rather than merely reflect them.

definition: A bounded momentum oscillator comparing average gains with average losses.
whyItMatters: It helps describe momentum regime, extension, and divergence.

sections.title: Formula
sections.body: RSI = 100 − 100/(1 + Average gain ÷ Average loss)

sections.title: Variables
sections.body: Average gain and average loss are smoothed positive and negative price changes over the chosen lookback, commonly 14 periods.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.body: An average gain twice the average loss produces an RSI near 66.7.

sections.title: Interpretation and limitation
sections.body: Overbought is not automatically bearish and oversold is not automatically bullish.

definition: Valuing a company by comparing multiples with peers, history, or transactions.
whyItMatters: Comparability and normalized fundamentals matter more than a low headline multiple.

definition: A price area where selling has previously been strong enough to slow an advance.
whyItMatters: Repeated tests can either validate the level or consume available supply.

definition: Monthly estimate of sales at retail and food-service businesses.
whyItMatters: Scheduled releases matter mainly through the surprise versus expectations and the change in the expected economic path.

sections.title: Publisher and cadence
sections.body: U.S. Census Bureau

sections.title: How to read it
sections.body: Compare the control group, revisions, price effects, and category breadth with expectations.

sections.title: Typical market channels
sections.body: Consumer discretionary and staples, GDP tracking, rates, card issuers, and logistics.

sections.title: Caution
sections.body: The release is nominal, excludes most services, and can be distorted by gasoline and autos.

definition: Cumulative profit retained in the business after dividends and certain adjustments.
whyItMatters: It shows historical reinvestment but not the current cash balance.

definition: A return to a recently broken level or boundary.
whyItMatters: A successful retest can clarify support, resistance, and invalidation.

definition: Net income generated relative to average total assets.
whyItMatters: It helps compare asset productivity within similar industries.

sections.title: Formula
sections.body: ROA = Net income ÷ Average total assets

sections.title: Variables
sections.body: Net income is bottom-line profit; average total assets is normally the mean of beginning and ending assets.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.body: $500M profit on $10B assets equals 5% ROA.

sections.title: Interpretation and limitation
sections.body: Asset intensity and accounting values differ widely across industries.

definition: Net income generated relative to average common equity.
whyItMatters: It measures owner-capital productivity but can be boosted by leverage.

sections.title: Formula
sections.body: ROE = Common net income ÷ Average common equity

sections.title: Variables
sections.body: Common net income is profit attributable to common owners; average common equity is normally the mean of beginning and ending common equity.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.body: $1B profit on $5B average equity equals 20% ROE.

sections.title: Interpretation and limitation
sections.body: Buybacks, write-downs, and high debt can shrink equity and inflate ROE.

definition: After-tax operating profit relative to capital invested in operations.
whyItMatters: ROIC versus cost of capital indicates whether growth creates economic value.

sections.title: Formula
sections.body: ROIC = NOPAT ÷ Average invested capital

sections.title: Variables
sections.body: NOPAT is net operating profit after tax; invested capital is the operating capital supplied by debt and equity holders, averaged when practical.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.body: $600M NOPAT on $4B invested capital equals 15% ROIC.

sections.title: Interpretation and limitation
sections.body: NOPAT and invested-capital adjustments must be consistent across companies and time.

definition: The value of goods or services recognized from ordinary business activity.
whyItMatters: Growth quality depends on price, volume, mix, timing, and collectability.

definition: A reduction in share count with a proportional increase in price per share.
whyItMatters: It changes trading units and may be used to meet listing requirements.

definition: The option price sensitivity to a change in interest rates.
whyItMatters: Rho matters more for longer-dated contracts and larger rate moves.

definition: An offer allowing existing shareholders to buy newly issued shares, often at a discount.
whyItMatters: Nonparticipating owners may be diluted.

definition: Price makes higher highs and higher lows inside two rising, converging boundaries.
whyItMatters: This bearish compression / breakout formation provides a structured way to define confirmation and invalidation.

sections.title: Confirmation
sections.body: Price closes below the lower wedge boundary with downside follow-through.

sections.title: Invalidation
sections.body: Price reclaims the lower boundary and breaks above the wedge high.

sections.title: Measured target
sections.body: Project the wedge’s widest height downward from the breakdown.

sections.title: Practical caution
sections.body: Treat the diagram as a schematic. Confirm the real price structure, timeframe, liquidity, and volume rather than matching a shape mechanically.

definition: A limit or allocation for how much portfolio risk an exposure may contribute.
whyItMatters: Risk budgeting prevents capital weights from disguising volatile positions.

definition: An investor's willingness and capacity to accept losses and uncertainty.
whyItMatters: A portfolio that exceeds tolerance is unlikely to be held through stress.

definition: Return evaluated relative to the risk taken to earn it.
whyItMatters: Raw returns can reward hidden leverage or concentration.

definition: A gradual saucer develops as a decline loses momentum and higher lows begin to appear.
whyItMatters: This bullish reversal formation provides a structured way to define confirmation and invalidation.

sections.title: Confirmation
sections.body: Price breaks the rim resistance after the right side of the saucer develops.

sections.title: Invalidation
sections.body: Price falls back below the rim and resumes making lower lows.

sections.title: Measured target
sections.body: Project the saucer depth upward from the rim break.

sections.title: Practical caution
sections.body: Treat the diagram as a schematic. Confirm the real price structure, timeframe, liquidity, and volume rather than matching a shape mechanically.

definition: A gradual dome develops as an advance loses momentum and lower highs begin to appear.
whyItMatters: This bearish reversal formation provides a structured way to define confirmation and invalidation.

sections.title: Confirmation
sections.body: Price breaks the base support after the right side of the dome develops.

sections.title: Invalidation
sections.body: Price recovers the base and resumes making higher highs.

sections.title: Measured target
sections.body: Project the dome depth downward from the base break.

sections.title: Practical caution
sections.body: Treat the diagram as a schematic. Confirm the real price structure, timeframe, liquidity, and volume rather than matching a shape mechanically.

definition: Sales growth from locations open for a defined comparable period.
whyItMatters: It separates existing-location performance from expansion.

definition: Evaluation of outcomes under coherent sets of assumptions.
whyItMatters: It makes uncertainty explicit instead of relying on one forecast.

definition: The market in which investors trade securities already issued.
whyItMatters: Most daily stock exchange activity occurs in the secondary market.

definition: A sale of additional shares by the company or existing holders after the IPO.
whyItMatters: Primary issuance raises capital and dilutes; holder sales do not fund the company.

definition: Long-duration growth driven by structural rather than cyclical forces.
whyItMatters: A secular tailwind can expand opportunity but may become overvalued.

definition: A tradable financial instrument representing ownership, debt, or a contractual right.
whyItMatters: The security type determines the holder's legal claim and risk exposure.

definition: Disclosure of financial results for distinct business components.
whyItMatters: Segments reveal different growth, margin, and capital characteristics hidden by totals.

definition: A table or process showing how an output changes when key assumptions change.
whyItMatters: It reveals which assumptions dominate a valuation conclusion.

definition: A company purchase of its own shares.
whyItMatters: Repurchases add value when executed below intrinsic value and funded prudently.

definition: All shares currently issued and held by investors, including restricted holdings.
whyItMatters: It is the denominator for per-share metrics and differs from public float.

definition: Excess return per unit of total return volatility.
whyItMatters: It compares reward with variability across strategies.

sections.title: Formula
sections.body: Sharpe = (Portfolio return − Risk-free rate) ÷ Return standard deviation

sections.title: Variables
sections.body: Portfolio return and risk-free rate use the same horizon; standard deviation is the volatility of portfolio returns over that horizon.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.body: An 8% excess return with 16% volatility gives a Sharpe ratio of 0.5.

sections.title: Interpretation and limitation
sections.body: It treats upside and downside volatility equally and can understate tail risk.

definition: A candle with a small body near the low and a long upper shadow after an advance.
whyItMatters: It can show rejection of higher prices when the next action confirms weakness.

definition: Shares sold short that remain open, usually reported as a quantity or percentage of float.
whyItMatters: High short interest can reflect bearish conviction and squeeze risk.

definition: A sale of borrowed shares with the intention of repurchasing them later.
whyItMatters: Losses can be theoretically unlimited if price rises.

definition: A rapid rise intensified by short sellers buying shares to close positions.
whyItMatters: Squeeze-driven prices can detach temporarily from fundamentals.

definition: A range-bound market without a sustained directional trend.
whyItMatters: Trend-following signals often whipsaw when price remains in a range.

definition: The arithmetic mean of prices over a fixed rolling window.
whyItMatters: It smooths noise and provides a lagging trend reference.

sections.title: Formula
sections.body: SMA(n) = Sum of last n prices ÷ n

sections.title: Variables
sections.body: n is the number of observations in the rolling window; prices are normally closes sampled at a consistent interval.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.body: Closing prices 10, 11, 12, 13, and 14 produce a five-period SMA of 12.

sections.title: Interpretation and limitation
sections.body: Window choice changes responsiveness; moving averages do not predict turning points.

definition: The difference between an expected execution price and the actual fill price.
whyItMatters: Slippage rises with volatility, order size, and weak liquidity.

definition: A slowdown that reduces inflation without a severe recession.
whyItMatters: The outcome can support earnings while allowing interest-rate pressure to ease.

definition: Excess return per unit of downside deviation.
whyItMatters: It focuses the risk penalty on returns below a selected target.

sections.title: Formula
sections.body: Sortino = (Portfolio return − Target return) ÷ Downside deviation

sections.title: Variables
sections.body: Portfolio return and target return use the same horizon; downside deviation measures returns falling below the target.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.body: A 6% excess return with 8% downside deviation gives 0.75.

sections.title: Interpretation and limitation
sections.body: Results depend on the target, data frequency, and limited tail observations.

definition: A nonrecurring distribution outside the normal dividend schedule.
whyItMatters: It can return excess capital but should not be annualized as ordinary income.

definition: Distribution of shares in a subsidiary or business to existing shareholders.
whyItMatters: Separate ownership can reveal value but creates standalone execution risks.

definition: A small-bodied candle with meaningful upper and lower shadows.
whyItMatters: It reflects two-sided trading and indecision rather than a complete signal.

definition: Weak growth combined with high inflation.
whyItMatters: It constrains policy choices and can pressure both margins and valuation.

definition: A momentum oscillator comparing the close with the recent high-low range.
whyItMatters: Overbought or oversold readings require trend context.

definition: An increase in share count with a proportional decrease in price per share.
whyItMatters: It changes trading units, not the company's total equity value by itself.

definition: Compensation paid with equity instruments or equity-linked awards.
whyItMatters: It is noncash when recorded but economically dilutes owners.

definition: An order that becomes a market order after a trigger price is reached.
whyItMatters: Fast markets can produce fills far from the stop price.

definition: An order that becomes a limit order after its stop price is reached.
whyItMatters: It controls the worst permitted price but can fail to execute.

definition: A call and put with the same strike and expiration, both long or both short.
whyItMatters: A long straddle needs a large move; a short straddle accepts substantial tail risk.

definition: A call and put with different strikes but the same expiration, both long or both short.
whyItMatters: It is cheaper than a comparable straddle when long but requires a larger move.

definition: An assessment of portfolio behavior under a severe hypothetical or historical scenario.
whyItMatters: It exposes nonlinear, concentrated, and liquidity risks hidden by averages.

definition: The contractual price at which an option may be exercised.
whyItMatters: Moneyness and payoff depend on the strike relative to the underlying.

definition: A method that values business segments separately and then combines them.
whyItMatters: It is useful when segments have different economics or appropriate peer groups.

definition: Allowing past, unrecoverable costs to influence a current decision.
whyItMatters: Future risk and reward should matter more than the original purchase price.

definition: A price area where buying has previously been strong enough to slow a decline.
whyItMatters: A break or hold can inform risk levels, but support is a zone rather than a guarantee.

definition: Studying only investments or funds that survived while ignoring failures.
whyItMatters: It overstates historical performance and strategy reliability.

definition: Lower highs and higher lows compress price toward an apex without confirming direction.
whyItMatters: This neutral compression / breakout formation provides a structured way to define confirmation and invalidation.

sections.title: Confirmation
sections.body: A close outside either boundary confirms direction; follow-through matters more than prediction.

sections.title: Invalidation
sections.body: Price immediately re-enters the triangle and crosses toward the opposite boundary.

sections.title: Measured target
sections.body: Project the triangle’s widest height in the confirmed breakout direction.

sections.title: Practical caution
sections.body: Treat the diagram as a schematic. Confirm the real price structure, timeframe, liquidity, and volume rather than matching a shape mechanically.

definition: Risk arising from broad market factors that diversification cannot remove.
whyItMatters: Equity beta, rates, and recessions can affect many holdings simultaneously.

definition: The risk of rare, extreme outcomes outside ordinary expectations.
whyItMatters: Leverage and liquidity mismatch can make tail events especially damaging.

definition: Study of price, volume, and market behavior to evaluate trend, momentum, and potential levels.
whyItMatters: It can structure entries and risk, but patterns are probabilistic rather than predictive certainties.

definition: A public offer to purchase shares directly from shareholders under specified terms.
whyItMatters: Terms, proration, conditions, and competing bids determine value.

definition: The estimated value of cash flows beyond an explicit forecast period.
whyItMatters: It often represents a large share of DCF value and demands conservative assumptions.

definition: The model-estimated change in option value from one day of time passing, all else equal.
whyItMatters: Option buyers generally pay and sellers generally collect time decay.

definition: The rule governing how long an order remains active.
whyItMatters: Choosing the wrong duration can create missed or unintended executions.

definition: The portion of an option premium above intrinsic value.
whyItMatters: It compensates the seller for the possibility of favorable movement before expiration.

definition: The maximum theoretical revenue opportunity for a product or service.
whyItMatters: It frames runway but can be overstated without realistic segmentation.

definition: The combined price change and distributions earned over a period.
whyItMatters: It is the correct basis for comparing investments that pay different income.

sections.title: Formula
sections.body: Total return = (Ending value − Beginning value + Distributions) ÷ Beginning value

sections.title: Variables
sections.body: Beginning and ending values refer to the investment value; distributions include cash dividends or other payouts received during the period.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.body: A move from $100 to $108 plus a $2 dividend produces a 10% total return.

sections.title: Interpretation and limitation
sections.body: Use adjusted prices and consistent treatment of reinvestment and taxes.

definition: The variability of a portfolio's return difference versus its benchmark.
whyItMatters: It measures active risk rather than whether active decisions were profitable.

definition: Monthly difference between exports and imports of goods and services.
whyItMatters: Scheduled releases matter mainly through the surprise versus expectations and the change in the expected economic path.

sections.title: Publisher and cadence
sections.body: Bureau of Economic Analysis and U.S. Census Bureau

sections.title: How to read it
sections.body: Inspect real versus nominal flows, petroleum, capital goods, and country or product concentration.

sections.title: Typical market channels
sections.body: GDP tracking, currencies, exporters, transport, and trade-policy narratives.

sections.title: Caution
sections.body: A narrower deficit can reflect weaker domestic demand rather than stronger competitiveness.

keywords: Bureau of Economic Analysis and U.S. Census Bureau

definition: A temporary suspension of trading in a security or market.
whyItMatters: Orders may face gap risk when trading resumes.

definition: The number of shares or contracts traded during a period.
whyItMatters: Volume helps assess liquidity and the participation behind a price move.

definition: A stop whose trigger follows favorable price movement by a fixed amount or percentage.
whyItMatters: It can protect gains while leaving room for a trend to continue.

definition: Debt issued by the U.S. federal government, including bills, notes, and bonds.
whyItMatters: Treasury yields are key benchmarks for risk-free rates and asset pricing.

definition: The prevailing direction and structure of price movement.
whyItMatters: Trading with or against the dominant trend changes expected win rate and risk.

definition: Three failed declines test a similar support zone with reaction highs between them.
whyItMatters: This bullish reversal formation provides a structured way to define confirmation and invalidation.

sections.title: Confirmation
sections.body: Price closes above the shared reaction-high resistance after the third trough.

sections.title: Invalidation
sections.body: Price establishes acceptance below the three-trough support zone.

sections.title: Measured target
sections.body: Project the resistance-to-support range upward from the resistance break.

sections.title: Practical caution
sections.body: Treat the diagram as a schematic. Confirm the real price structure, timeframe, liquidity, and volume rather than matching a shape mechanically.

definition: Three failed pushes test a similar resistance zone with reaction lows between them.
whyItMatters: This bearish reversal formation provides a structured way to define confirmation and invalidation.

sections.title: Confirmation
sections.body: Price closes beneath the shared reaction-low support after the third peak.

sections.title: Invalidation
sections.body: Price establishes acceptance above the three-peak resistance zone.

sections.title: Measured target
sections.body: Project the resistance-to-support range downward from the support break.

sections.title: Practical caution
sections.body: Treat the diagram as a schematic. Confirm the real price structure, timeframe, liquidity, and volume rather than matching a shape mechanically.

definition: Trading volume expressed relative to shares outstanding or float.
whyItMatters: Turnover makes activity more comparable across companies of different sizes.

definition: Revenue and costs associated with one customer, product, or transaction unit.
whyItMatters: Attractive unit economics are essential when growth requires repeated acquisition spending.

definition: Preliminary and final monthly survey of consumer sentiment and inflation expectations.
whyItMatters: Scheduled releases matter mainly through the surprise versus expectations and the change in the expected economic path.

sections.title: Publisher and cadence
sections.body: University of Michigan

sections.title: How to read it
sections.body: Markets focus on changes in one-year and long-run inflation expectations as well as sentiment.

sections.title: Typical market channels
sections.body: Rates, policy expectations, consumer sectors, and inflation narratives.

sections.title: Caution
sections.body: The sample is smaller than hard spending data and preliminary figures can be revised.

definition: A short-sale restriction that can apply after a significant one-day decline.
whyItMatters: It limits certain short executions during acute downward pressure.

definition: A price structure generally characterized by higher highs and higher lows.
whyItMatters: A broken sequence can warn that trend strength is changing.

definition: An estimate of the loss threshold not expected to be exceeded at a chosen confidence level and horizon.
whyItMatters: It summarizes ordinary tail exposure but says little about losses beyond the threshold.

definition: Seeking securities priced below a reasoned estimate of intrinsic value.
whyItMatters: The approach depends on valuation quality and patience, not merely low multiples.

definition: The option price sensitivity to a one-percentage-point change in implied volatility.
whyItMatters: Long-dated and near-the-money options often carry substantial vega.

definition: Long and short options of the same type and expiration at different strikes.
whyItMatters: It defines maximum gain and loss while reducing premium relative to a single leg.

definition: The degree and speed of price variation over time.
whyItMatters: Volatility affects position sizing, option prices, and expected drawdowns.

definition: The average traded price weighted by volume during a chosen period.
whyItMatters: VWAP is a common intraday benchmark and institutional execution reference.

definition: A long-dated issuer-created right to purchase shares at a specified price.
whyItMatters: Exercise can create new shares and dilute existing owners.

definition: A monitored list of securities that are not necessarily owned.
whyItMatters: It supports disciplined preparation before a price or thesis trigger occurs.

definition: The blended required return of debt and equity capital weighted by market values.
whyItMatters: It is commonly used to discount unlevered free cash flow.

sections.title: Formula
sections.body: WACC = E/(D+E)×Cost of equity + D/(D+E)×After-tax cost of debt

sections.title: Variables
sections.body: E and D are market values of equity and debt; each cost is the required return for that capital source; debt cost is reduced by the applicable tax shield.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.body: With 80% equity at 10% and 20% debt at 4% after tax, WACC is 8.8%.

sections.title: Interpretation and limitation
sections.body: Capital structure, beta, tax, country risk, and cyclicality make WACC uncertain.

definition: An unofficial expectation that may differ from the published consensus.
whyItMatters: A stock can fall after an official beat if investors expected more.

definition: Current operating assets minus current operating liabilities, or more broadly current assets minus current liabilities.
whyItMatters: Changes in working capital can consume or release cash.

definition: The relationship between yields and maturities for comparable debt securities.
whyItMatters: Its level and shape reflect policy, growth, inflation, and term-premium expectations.

definition: A condition in which shorter-term yields exceed longer-term yields.
whyItMatters: It has preceded many recessions but provides uncertain timing.
